extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and screenwriters (authors of stories/screenplays)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and analyzing stories and screenplays (character, structure, scenes, pacing, genre, plot devices, and craft techniques). Geared toward improving/assessing narrative fiction for film and prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (creation and truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character — first step in creating; true character versus mere characterization; biography/backstory; dimension; comic character; revelation; relationship to climax and arc; 'Character as destiny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters with biography and backstory that support true, multidimensional behavior; craft arcs tied to the story's climax; treat comic and dramatic functions distinctly; consider cast size and each character's function in structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist (role and development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist — relation to audience bond; active vs. passive protagonist; spine (through-line/superobjective); single vs. multiple protagonists; multiprotagonist and plural protagonists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the protagonist's through-line drives the story; create strong audience identification; decide whether single or multiple protagonists suit the narrative and structure the spine accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling Idea (theme/central proposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlling Idea — components, relationship to climax and endings, ironic variants, counter-ideas and subplots, role in the creative process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate a clear controlling idea that the plot tests and expresses; use it to shape climax and ending; consider ironic or counter-ideas to deepen thematic complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of story (design and types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure — classical design; five-part/three-act design; Archplot, Miniplot, Antiplot; causality vs. coincidence; change vs. stasis; linear vs. nonlinear time; closed vs. open endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a structural mode appropriate to genre and intention; maintain causal logic (or deliberately subvert it) and be consistent about time and reality; match structure to desired ending (closed/open).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident (creation and placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inciting Incident — locating and designing the inciting event; relation to act design, flashback, quality of inciting incident, and its role in propelling the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a distinct, consequential inciting incident early enough to set the story in motion; ensure it forces the protagonist into action and connects to later turning points and the spine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax and Endings (design and types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Climax — last-act climax, mid-act climax, sequence climax; positive/negative; ironic/endings (ironic, idealistic, pessimistic); reversal; relation to character self-recognition and controlling idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build the climax to resolve the controlling idea and protagonist's arc; choose an ending tone (closed/open/ironic) consistent with story values; place crises and reversals to maximize dramatic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning Points and Points of No Return
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning Points — critical scenes that change direction; points of no return and their placement; relation to choices, backstory, and escalation toward climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure turning points to escalate stakes and force irrevocable choices; use them to reshape the protagonist's path and maintain momentum toward the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene Design and Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes — French scenes, opening/closing value, crisis scenes, emotional transitions, length and number of scenes, setups/playoffs, key images, scene analysis specifics and how scenes build toward climaxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes with clear opening/closing values and emotional trajectory; use setups and payoffs; analyze scenes for beats, turning points, and contribution to the spine; avoid 'pointless pace killers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot and Multiplot (integration and resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplot/Multiplot — relationship with main plot, how subplots resolve, multilevel plots and multiprotagonist dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave subplots to support or contrast the controlling idea; ensure they have their own arcs and contribute to overall resolution rather than distracting from the main spine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre Conventions and Audience Expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres — lists and conventions for crime, thriller, comedy, melodrama, western, horror, fantasy, etc.; relationship of genre to setting, audience expectations, and creative limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect and/or knowingly subvert genre conventions; design story elements (tone, setup, obligatory scenes) to meet or play against audience expectations while maintaining originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict (law of conflict and levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict — Law of Conflict; three levels of conflict; principle of complication through complexity; external vs. internal conflict; conflict and scene analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create escalating, layered conflicts (internal, interpersonal, societal); use complication and complexity to deepen stakes; ensure conflicts are woven into structure and scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression (complication vs. complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Progression — personal, social, symbolic ascension; law of diminishing returns; progression through escalating complications toward crisis and climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot complications should escalate meaningfully; avoid repetitive rises without consequence; use progression to move the protagonist from stasis to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Arc (risk, maturity, revelation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character arc — arc and revelation, risk and maturity, gap between character and world, self-recognition tied to climax, and backstory's role in arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design an arc where the protagonist must risk or mature to resolve the controlling idea; reveal key backstory only as needed to support choices and recognition at climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue (craft and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue — short speeches, silent screenplay strategies, suspense sentence, when to begin writing dialogue, and dialogue's relationship to description and image systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep dialogue economical and purposeful; use short speeches for momentum; utilize silence and subtext; craft 'suspense sentences' to propel scenes; integrate dialogue with visual imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and Image Systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Description and image systems — how descriptive writing and recurring images build meaning; use of image systems across scenes and sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop image systems (repeated motifs/objects) that reinforce theme and character; make description functional—revealing character, setting, or symbolic weight rather than inert detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing, Rhythm, and Tempo
rubrics_metrics.description: Pacing — scene length and number, rhythm and tempo, law of diminishing returns, 'pointless pace killer,' and composition expressing progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control pacing through scene length, beats, and transitions; vary rhythm for emotional effect; avoid repetitive pacing that reduces impact; use tempo to escalate toward climaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and Transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition — expressing progression, transition/Third Thing, unity and variety, transitions between scenes, and build of sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose scenes to show progression; use transitions like the 'Third Thing' to bridge beats without flattening pace; aim for unity with variety across scenes and sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setups and Payoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Setups/Playoffs — establishing elements early that pay off later (key images, obligatory scenes, sequence climaxes), and how to place them across story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant setups deliberately and ensure satisfying payoffs; use obligatory scenes where genre or story logic requires them; distribute setups to build toward sequence and act climaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligatory Scene (fulfillment of story promise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obligatory Scene — scenes that the story must deliver (genre or premise-driven) and their placement relative to crisis and climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and design obligatory scenes early; ensure they occur where they deliver maximum dramatic and thematic value and fulfill audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal and Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal — structural reversals, penultimate reversals, reversal of fortune; Surprise — cheap versus earned surprise, and use of coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals that are motivated and consistent with character; prefer earned surprises over cheap twists; avoid reliance on coincidence unless justified and foreshadowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony (dramatic and in endings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony — dramatic irony, ironic endings and ascension, negative and ironic ascension, and how irony relates to controlling idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ irony to deepen thematic resonance; align ironic outcomes with the controlling idea; don't use irony gratuitously—make it emerge from story logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of View (POV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of View — character POV vs. shot POV (film), voice choices, and how POV shapes audience identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and sustain a POV that serves the spine; use POV shifts deliberately and transparently; align cinematic shot POVs to narrative POV for coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting (worldbuilding and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting — duration, location, period, values/rituals of a setting world, politics of the story world, and creative limitations imposed by setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design settings that constrain and enable action; use rituals and values to generate conflict; let setting inform character choices and thematic stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and Style (voice and vividness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style — adding vividness, tips on style, voice-over narration, poetry/image use, treating the writer as poet, and when to begin writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a consistent stylistic voice that enhances images and scenes; utilize voice-over or poetic devices sparingly and purposefully to avoid undercutting dramatic immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure Elements: Spine, Premise, and Theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Spine (through-line/superobjective), premise, and how these shape scene choices, arcs, and controlling idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate the spine and premise early; let them determine scene selection and character objectives so every scene advances the through-line toward thematic resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts and Act Design
rubrics_metrics.description: Act design — placement of inciting incident, mid-act climax, sequence climax, number of scenes per act, and act rhythm (e.g., five-part designs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design acts with turning points and climaxes that escalate conflict; balance scene distribution and place crises to maximize tension and propel to next act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence and Sequence Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence — grouping of scenes into sequences and designing sequence climaxes that contribute to act and story climaxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose sequences as mini-arcs with their own crises and climaxes that feed the larger act and narrative climaxes; use them to maintain momentum and thematic focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backstory and Flashback (use and withholding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Backstory — role in character birth and motivation; flashback placement; withholding information and pacing of exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal backstory only as it becomes necessary to explain actions or deepen stakes; avoid expository dumps; use flashback sparingly and purposefully to reframe choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Research — factual research vs. imagination vs. memory; research's role in authentic character birth and progressive complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground fiction in researched detail where necessary for credibility, but prioritize imaginative truth; blend memory and fact to create believable character backgrounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations of Commercial/Studio Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Hollywood/Commercial considerations — big hook, budget constraints, number of films produced, studio development processes, story analyst expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing commercially, tailor premise, hook, and structure to marketplace realities; be mindful of budgetary and studio storytelling conventions without surrendering craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step-outline, Treatment, and Pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-production documents — step-outline, expansion, treatment, screenplay length, and pitch considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use outlines and treatments to test structure and spine before full drafting; craft pitches to clearly express premise, hook, and controlling idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image Keys and Key Images
rubrics_metrics.description: Key Images — recurring or striking images that anchor theme and emotional resonance across the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and repeat images that symbolically support the controlling idea; ensure they advance plot or character rather than serving as mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligatory Beats and Scene Beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Beats — the smallest dramatic units within scenes; their role in scene progression and emotional transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write clear beats with turning values to keep scenes active; sequence beats to build to scene climax and then transition to next scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing and Revision (problem of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing plot — problem of interest, testing plot ideas, and dealing with lack of interest or clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively test plot through outlines/readings; remove clichés and 'pointless pace killers'; sharpen inciting incidents, stakes, and reversals to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text vs. Subtext (layering meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Text and subtext — how dialogue/action surface (text) and underlying motives/themes (subtext) interplay across scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer subtext under dialogue and action to create depth; ensure subtextual meaning is supported by scene setups and payoffs, not just hinted at vaguely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligatory and False Mysteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery types — closed vs. open mysteries, false mysteries, red herrings, and cliffhangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mysteries and red herrings to sustain curiosity but make sure solutions feel earned; avoid contrived false mysteries that cheat audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and Avoiding Cliché
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding cliché — recognizing clichés in action, transition, and climax; principle of creative limitation to force originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constrain choices (creative limitation) to provoke original approaches; resist clichés through research, specificity, and surprising yet plausible turns.
